title: The collect for peace (1662)
hook: give unto thy servants that peace which the world cannot give
tomorrow: what do you say standing at the edge of a grave?

segments.voice: Yesterday the prayer book's thank-you note named creation, preservation, and all the blessings of this life.

Noise-canceling headphones, a do-not-disturb setting, a quiet room booked for an hour: peace you can buy or arrange. Evening Prayer in the 1662 prayer book ends with three short prayers, and the second asks for something odd. Not a quieter street, not a calmer week. It asks God for "that peace which the world cannot give." And here's the strange detail: before it asks for peace at all, it talks about desires, counsels and works.
screen: `PEACE YOU CAN ARRANGE.` → `PEACE THE WORLD CAN'T GIVE.` → `WHY START WITH DESIRES?`

segments.voice: A collect is a short, set prayer, and this one has a shape you can see. It doesn't start by asking. It starts by naming where good things come from: "O God, from whom all holy desires, all good counsels, and all just works do proceed: Give unto thy servants that peace which the world cannot give." Desires, counsels, works: wanting the good, choosing it, doing it. All three, it says, start with God. That's the puzzle's first answer: the peace comes from the same place as wanting the good at all. Then the borrowed phrase. At the Last Supper in John's Gospel, Jesus tells his friends: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you." The collect turns that into a request. Then it says what the peace is for: hearts set to obey God's commandments, and, defended from the fear of enemies, time passed in rest and quietness. Look at the order. The quiet comes last. One way Christians read it: the world's peace arrives when the trouble leaves. This prayer asks for a peace that can come first, while the trouble is still in the room.
screen: `DESIRES, COUNSELS, WORKS.` · `NOT AS THE WORLD GIVETH.` · `THE QUIET COMES LAST.` · `PEACE BEFORE THE TROUBLE LEAVES.` · then, large: `PEACE THE WORLD CANNOT GIVE.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly across the room and back as the sit begins. With each step, bring to mind one place where peace feels thin, a conversation, a worry, a person, and let the phrase walk beside it: peace which the world cannot give. Sit when you're ready; if you pray, you can say the collect's line once, quietly.
The collect for peace. The prayer book's evening request for a peace that's given, not arranged.
Your line: peace the world cannot give, the kind that can arrive before the trouble leaves. Goodnight.

screen: `DAY 1647 COUNTS.` → `THE SAINTS IN THEIR OWN WORDS · 46 OF 80.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DO YOU SAY STANDING AT THE EDGE OF A GRAVE?`

howItsDone: In the 1662 prayer book this collect is said near the end of Evening Prayer, and Anglican and Episcopal churches still pray it, or a version of it, at evening services.

chat.says: nia's great-grandma died last night, in her sleep. everyone tells nia 'she's at peace.' nia says SHE isn't.
options: Don't rush her. The prayer book's peace isn't grief gone; it can come while trouble stays.
Tell her she will be soon. Peace comes once the funeral's done and things settle.
Tell her not to be sad, since being upset means she hasn't found peace yet.
